title: Trump Administration Escalates Legal Battles Ahead of Midterms, Laying Groundwork to Contest Results
snippet: With polls forecasting potential defeat, President Donald Trump's Justice Department is aggressively deploying lawsuits and probes that could delay and challenge election results past Election Day.
content:
WASHINGTON — Facing an uphill battle to maintain control of Congress, President Donald Trump and his Justice Department are mounting an unprecedented legal blitz across key states, launching investigations and filing last-minute lawsuits that legal scholars say are designed to prolong disputes well past Election Day.

The administration's aggressive maneuvers mark a sharp departure from traditional Department of Justice protocol, which historically avoids high-profile, politically sensitive legal actions in the final weeks before an election. Instead, federal prosecutors are seeking to force states to set aside thousands of ballots, challenge voter eligibility, and threaten local election administrators with criminal prosecution if they certify certain results.

Federal Courts Rebuff California Voter Challenges

The administration's strategy has suffered immediate setbacks in court. In California, federal prosecutors sought to halt the counting of more than 20,000 ballots cast by voters suspected of being noncitizens, warning local election officials they could face criminal charges for aiding illegal voting.

Federal judges swiftly rejected the department's arguments. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter cautioned federal officials against threatening local workers, writing that the plan likely violated the Voting Rights Act. His ruling was subsequently upheld by a Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel, which noted that the Justice Department holds no constitutional authority to intervene in ongoing state-run elections. Additionally, U.S. District Judge Trina L. Thompson issued an emergency order barring federal authorities from making further demands or threatening poll workers in the state.

Unprecedented Interference in Alaska Senate Race

In Alaska, the department is pursuing a novel legal tactic aimed at stalling the finalization of the state's Senate race if Democratic incumbent Mary Peltola wins. Justice Department lawyers claim voters may be confused by another candidate on the ballot, Dan J. Sullivan, who shares a nearly identical name with the Republican incumbent, Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.

Relying on an unheard-of interpretation of the National Voter Registration Act, federal attorneys have asked a judge to order the state to segregate ballots and withhold certification pending an investigation. State legal representatives have urged the court to reject the maneuver, characterizing it as an unconstitutional attempt to exert federal control over state electoral procedures.

A Transformed Justice Department

The wave of late litigation follows a major restructuring within the Justice Department under Attorney General Todd Blanche. Longtime career prosecutors within the Civil Rights Division have departed or been replaced by political appointees, shifting the department's focus away from protecting ballot access and toward aggressive voter eligibility probes.

While administration officials insist the probes are vital to preserving election integrity, voting rights advocates view the efforts as a calculated attempt to cast doubt on election outcomes in advance.

"A lot of what you are seeing is just a sort of temper tantrum in the form of a lawsuit," said Sam Oliker-Friedland, executive director of the Institute for Responsive Government. With dozens of cases continuing to wind through federal courts, the legal battles threaten to extend the 2026 midterm fights long after the polls close.
